scenes.kicker: F08 · Derivatives and Risk Management · Module 3
scenes.head: Hedging with derivatives
scenes.sub: A hedge rarely matches the exposure perfectly. Work out how many futures contracts minimise the risk when the futures track a related price, measure what the hedge leaves behind, follow basis risk through a grower’s hedge, change a portfolio’s market exposure with index futures, and choose between futures and options.

segs.say: Hedging with derivatives. A hedge rarely matches the exposure perfectly. Work out how many futures contracts minimise the risk when the futures track a related price, measure what the hedge leaves behind, follow basis risk through a grower’s hedge, change a portfolio’s market exposure with index futures, and choose between futures and options.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate the minimum-variance hedge ratio and the number of futures contracts for a hedge, and the share of risk the hedge removes.
Explain basis risk, and calculate the effective price a hedger locks in when the basis changes.
Calculate the number of index futures contracts needed to change a portfolio’s beta.
Compare hedges with forwards, futures and options, including collars, by cost, protection and what is given up.
Evaluate a hedge against a written hedging policy, including cross hedges and over-hedging.

scenes.head: Lantern is too small for futures, as lesson 2 showed, but Brightcup is not.

segs.say: Lantern is too small for futures, as lesson 2 showed, but Brightcup is not. Its treasurer, whose swap Ana followed in lesson 4, now wants to hedge next quarter’s purchases of roasted coffee, about $6,000,000, with the fictional green-coffee futures. Roasted coffee is not green coffee, so the futures will not track Brightcup’s costs exactly. Meanwhile Hollis, with $500,000 in listed investments, asks whether he could reduce his exposure to the stock market for a few months without selling anything.

chapters.title: When the hedge does not match the exposure

scenes.head: A hedge is perfect only when the contract is on exactly the asset being hedged, for exactly the quantity and date.

segs.say: A hedge is perfect only when the contract is on exactly the asset being hedged, for exactly the quantity and date. More often the contract is on something related: green coffee for roasted coffee, a share index for a portfolio, crude oil for jet fuel. This is a cross hedge, and the question becomes how much of the contract to use. Hedging one for one is not necessarily best, because the two prices do not move by the same amounts.

scenes.head: Brightcup’s analysts estimated, from three years of quarterly data (fictional), that its roasted-coffee prices change with a standard deviation of 6%…

segs.say: Brightcup’s analysts estimated, from three years of quarterly data (fictional), that its roasted-coffee prices change with a standard deviation of 6% a quarter, the futures price with 9%, and the correlation between the two changes is 0.85. The futures move more than Brightcup’s costs, and not always together.

scenes.head: Choose the hedge ratio h (units of futures per unit of exposure, in value) to make the hedged position’s variance as small as possible.

segs.say: Choose the hedge ratio h (units of futures per unit of exposure, in value) to make the hedged position’s variance as small as possible. A little calculus, or a regression of the change in the spot price on the change in the futures price, gives the minimum-variance hedge ratio:
For Brightcup, h* = 0.85 × 0.06 ÷ 0.09 = 0.5667. Each futures contract covers 5,000 kg at $6.40, $32,000 of coffee, so the number of contracts is:

scenes.head: Brightcup buys 106 contracts.

segs.say: Brightcup buys 106 contracts. (It buys because it is exposed to a rise in the price it pays.) The share of the variance the hedge removes, its hedge effectiveness, is ρ² = 72.25%.
Risk left in next quarter’s coffee bill ($6.0 million), one standard deviation (dollars)

scenes.head: The minimum-variance hedge cuts the risk from $360,000 to $189,642.

segs.say: The minimum-variance hedge cuts the risk from $360,000 to $189,642. The one-for-one hedge leaves more, $301,198, because it adds the futures’ own extra volatility. The risk that remains, σS√(1 − ρ²), is basis risk in its general form: the part of the price that the futures do not track.

chapters.title: Basis risk in a single hedge

scenes.head: Even a hedge on the right commodity carries basis risk, because the hedger usually closes the futures before delivery, and the gap between spot and…

segs.say: Even a hedge on the right commodity carries basis risk, because the hedger usually closes the futures before delivery, and the gap between spot and futures prices on that day is not known in advance. The basis is the spot price less the futures price.

scenes.head: A growers’ cooperative sells futures at $6.40 when the spot price is $6.30 (basis -0.10), to protect the price of a crop it will sell in a few months.

segs.say: A growers’ cooperative sells futures at $6.40 when the spot price is $6.30 (basis -0.10), to protect the price of a crop it will sell in a few months. When it sells the crop, the spot price is $5.90 and the futures $6.05 (basis -0.15). It sells the crop for $5.90 and gains 6.40 − 6.05 = $0.35 a kg on the futures, an effective price of $6.25.
Effective price = S₁ + (F₀ − F₁) = F₀ + b₁

scenes.head: The effective price is the futures price when the hedge was set plus the basis when it is lifted: 6.40 + (-0.15) = $6.25.

segs.say: The effective price is the futures price when the hedge was set plus the basis when it is lifted: 6.40 + (-0.15) = $6.25. The futures locked in $6.40; the only uncertainty left is the closing basis. Here the basis weakened by 0.05, costing the seller 0.05 a kg against what it might have expected. A buyer would have gained from the same change. Basis risk is usually much smaller than the price risk it replaces, which is why hedgers accept it.

chapters.title: Hedging a share portfolio with index futures

scenes.head: Hollis’s book is $42,000 in Brightcup, $308,000 in the Harbourline market fund and $150,000 in a bond fund.

segs.say: Hollis’s book is $42,000 in Brightcup, $308,000 in the Harbourline market fund and $150,000 in a bond fund. Using F06’s betas (Brightcup 1.05, the bond fund 0.13 on the simulated data, the market fund 1 by definition), the book’s beta is 0.7431: it moves about 74 cents for each dollar the market moves, per dollar invested.

scenes.head: A fictional index futures contract on the Harbourline index is worth 5,000 points × $50 = $250,000.

segs.say: A fictional index futures contract on the Harbourline index is worth 5,000 points × $50 = $250,000. Selling index futures lowers the book’s beta without selling any investments. To remove the market exposure entirely:
N = β_P (V_P)/(F × m)

N = 0.7431 × 500,000 ÷ 250,000 = 1.49 contracts. Contracts are whole, so Hollis could sell one, cutting his beta to 0.7431 − 250,000 ÷ 500,000 = 0.2431, or two, which would take it slightly below zero. To move to a target beta β*, sell (βP − β*) × VP ÷ (F × m) contracts. An index hedge removes market risk only: the risk specific to Brightcup, the part of its movements that the market does not explain, stays with him.

scenes.head: The choice of instrument depends on what the hedger is willing to give up.

segs.say: The choice of instrument depends on what the hedger is willing to give up. Forwards and futures fix the price: they remove the bad outcomes and the good ones, and cost nothing up front beyond margin. Options remove only the bad outcomes, and cost a premium. A collar sits between them: it buys a put and pays for it by writing a call, setting both a floor and a ceiling.

scenes.head: Hollis could collar his Brightcup shares by buying the $40 put at $2.18 and writing the $46 call at $2.37.

segs.say: Hollis could collar his Brightcup shares by buying the $40 put at $2.18 and writing the $46 call at $2.37. The call brings in more than the put costs: a net credit of $0.19 a share, $190 on 1,000 shares. On 31 March 2029 his shares are worth between $40,000 and $46,000, whatever Brightcup does. He gives up gains above $46 to pay for protection below $40.
Choosing a hedge

scenes.head: In practice h* is estimated by regressing past changes in the price being hedged on changes in the futures price over the same periods: the slope of…

segs.say: In practice h* is estimated by regressing past changes in the price being hedged on changes in the futures price over the same periods: the slope of the line is h*, and the regression’s R² is the hedge effectiveness. The periods should match the hedge’s horizon (quarterly changes for a quarterly hedge), and the data should be recent enough to reflect how the two prices move together now. Brightcup’s analysts used three years of quarters; a longer history gives a steadier estimate but may include years when the relation was different. Hedge accounting rules ask for the same evidence: a documented, reasonable expectation that the hedge will offset most of the exposure.

scenes.head: Pulling the course together for Lantern: its coffee is hedged by Kilnworth’s fixed price, a forward that matches the exact quantity, grade and dates…

segs.say: Pulling the course together for Lantern: its coffee is hedged by Kilnworth’s fixed price, a forward that matches the exact quantity, grade and dates; its €38,000 bill by Coastline’s currency forward; its debt needs no swap because the term loan is fixed and the line of credit is being repaid. It looked at futures and at a price cap and chose not to use them: futures because the contracts are too large and of the wrong grade, the cap because Ana valued certainty more than the chance of cheaper coffee. Each choice follows the same steps: measure the exposure, choose the instrument that fits it best, decide how much to hedge, and know what risk is left.

scenes.head: A few practical points decide whether a hedge works as designed.

segs.say: A few practical points decide whether a hedge works as designed. Hedge ratios estimated from past data change, so they should be re-estimated and the hedge adjusted from time to time. Long exposures are often hedged by rolling short-dated futures forward, closing each contract before delivery and opening the next, which adds a basis risk at each roll. Futures hedges need cash for margin calls, as lesson 2 showed. And a hedge should be checked against the policy that authorised it: the exposure it covers, the share hedged, the instruments allowed and the limits. A position larger than the exposure, or in an instrument with little connection to it, is a speculation however it is labelled.

scenes.head: Minimum-variance hedge ratio

segs.say: Minimum-variance hedge ratio: h^* = ρ (σ_S)/(σ_F).
h^*: Units of futures per unit of exposure.
ρ: Correlation between changes in the spot and futures prices.
σ_S: Standard deviation of changes in the spot price (or its proportional changes).
σ_F: Standard deviation of changes in the futures price, on the same basis.
Equal to the slope of a regression of spot changes on futures changes. Hedge effectiveness is ρ².

scenes.head: Number of futures contracts

segs.say: Number of futures contracts: N^* = h^* (V_A)/(V_F).
N^*: Number of futures contracts.
h^*: The minimum-variance hedge ratio.
V_A: Value of the exposure ($).
V_F: Value of one futures contract (size × price) ($).

scenes.head: Effective price with a futures hedge

segs.say: Effective price with a futures hedge: S₁ + (F₀ − F₁) = F₀ + b₁.
S₁: Spot price when the hedge is lifted ($).
F₀, F₁: Futures price when the hedge is set and lifted ($).
b₁: Basis when the hedge is lifted, S₁ − F₁ ($).
For a short hedge (a seller). A buyer’s effective cost is the same expression.

scenes.head: Index futures to change a portfolio’s beta

segs.say: Index futures to change a portfolio’s beta: N = (β_P − β^*) (V_P)/(F × m).
N: Number of index futures contracts to sell.
β_P, β^*: The portfolio’s beta now and the target.
V_P: Value of the portfolio ($).
F: Index futures price (points).
m: Dollars a point (the multiplier) ($).
A positive N means sell contracts.

scenes.head: The grower’s effective price

segs.say: A cooperative sells futures at $6.40 with spot at $6.30. It lifts the hedge when spot is $5.90 and futures $6.05. Find the effective price and the change in the basis.

scenes.head: The grower’s effective price

segs.say: Step 1. Futures gain: 6.40 − 6.05 = 0.35 a kg.
Step 2. Effective price: 5.90 + 0.35 = 6.25.
Step 4. The basis moved from -0.10 to -0.15, a weakening of 0.05.

scenes.head: The grower’s effective price

segs.say: Without the hedge the cooperative would have received $5.90; the hedge recovered most of the fall, less the basis change.

scenes.head: Halving Hollis’s market exposure

segs.say: Hollis’s $500,000 book has a beta of 0.7431. Index futures are at 5,000 with a $50 multiplier. How many contracts would halve his beta, and what can he actually do?

scenes.head: Halving Hollis’s market exposure

segs.say: Step 1. Target β* = 0.3716.
Step 3. Whole contracts: selling 1 gives β = 0.2431, close to the target.

scenes.head: Halving Hollis’s market exposure

segs.say: Sell 1 contract; his beta falls to about 0.2431.
Index futures change market exposure cheaply and quickly, but in steps of $250,000; smaller investors may use index options or funds instead.

scenes.head: Minimum-variance hedge for Brightcup’s coffee

segs.say: The minimum-variance hedge for Brightcup’s coffee. Change the correlation and the two volatilities and see the hedge ratio, the contracts and the risk left, against hedging one for one. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Hollis’s index futures hedge

segs.say: Hollis’s index hedge. Sell from zero to three contracts and see his beta and how much a 10% fall in the market would cost him. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Hedging one for one by default

segs.say: Hedging one for one by default. When the futures are more volatile than the exposure, or imperfectly correlated with it, a one-for-one hedge adds risk. Use h* = ρσS/σF.

scenes.head: Mixing price changes and proportional changes

segs.say: Mixing price changes and proportional changes. Estimate σS, σF and ρ on the same basis. With proportional changes, multiply h* by the value of the exposure over the value of a contract.

scenes.head: Thinking a futures hedge removes all risk

segs.say: Thinking a futures hedge removes all risk. It replaces price risk with basis risk: the effective price is F0 plus the basis when the hedge is lifted.

scenes.head: Using an index hedge for a single share’s risk

segs.say: Using an index hedge for a single share’s risk. Index futures remove market risk. A share’s own risk, the part not explained by the market, remains.

scenes.head: Forgetting that a collar caps the upside

segs.say: Forgetting that a collar caps the upside. A zero-cost collar is not free: its cost is the gains given up above the call’s strike.

scenes.head: Airlines are the classic cross hedgers: jet fuel has few liquid futures, so many airlines hedge with crude oil or heating oil futures and options…

segs.say: Airlines are the classic cross hedgers: jet fuel has few liquid futures, so many airlines hedge with crude oil or heating oil futures and options, and accept the basis risk between them. Food companies hedge grains with futures on the nearest traded grade; exporters hedge currencies with forwards; fund managers adjust their market exposure with index futures rather than selling shares, which would take longer and cost more. In each case the questions in this lesson are asked: which contract tracks the exposure best, how many contracts, and what risk remains.

scenes.head: Hedging can also fail spectacularly when the hedge and the exposure differ in timing or in cash.

segs.say: Hedging can also fail spectacularly when the hedge and the exposure differ in timing or in cash. A company that hedges long-dated supply contracts with short-dated futures, rolling them over each month, can face large margin calls when prices fall, while its gains on the supply contracts arrive only over years. The economics may be sound and the company may still run out of cash, as lesson 2 warned. Good hedging programmes plan for the cash needed in the worst months, not only for the average outcome.

scenes.head: Accounting matters as well.

segs.say: Accounting matters as well. Under hedge accounting (ASC 815 in US GAAP, IFRS 9 elsewhere) a company must document the hedge relationship and show that the hedge is expected to be effective; the ratio and correlation in this lesson are the evidence. Ineffective portions of a hedge go to profit as they arise.

scenes.head: Brightcup buys 106 contracts, and Hollis sells one index contract for the three months until Brightcup’s results, bringing his beta to about 0.2431.

segs.say: Brightcup buys 106 contracts, and Hollis sells one index contract for the three months until Brightcup’s results, bringing his beta to about 0.2431. Ana notes that both hedges need cash for margin, and that Hollis’s hedge is now partly leverage in reverse. The next lesson looks at margin and leverage directly, and at the short sales that index futures make unnecessary.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: In a cross hedge the minimum-variance hedge ratio is h* = ρσS/σF; the contracts are h* × VA ÷ VF.
Hedge effectiveness is ρ²; the risk left is σS√(1 − ρ²) of the exposure.
A futures hedge locks in F0 plus the basis at the close: price risk becomes basis risk.
Index futures change a portfolio’s beta: sell (βP − β*) × VP ÷ (F × m) contracts.
Forwards and futures fix prices; options keep the upside for a premium; collars trade the upside for cheap protection.
A hedge should match a policy: the exposure, the share hedged, the instruments and the limits.
